Netflix Offered Xbox $500 Million for Seven Years of Film and TV Rights, and Xbox Asked for $800 Million
Bela Bajaria offered Microsoft $500 million for seven years of exclusive Xbox film and TV adaptation rights, Xbox countered at $800 million, and Netflix pulled the offer after Bajaria was fired.
Puck's Matthew Belloni reports, citing three sources, that Netflix chief content officer Bela Bajaria recently offered Microsoft $500 million to license Xbox titles exclusively for film and TV adaptations over seven years. Xbox's Asha Sharma and her business affairs team countered at $800 million. With Bajaria gone, Netflix has taken the offer off the table; chief financial officer Spence Neumann was among those who thought it too high. Xbox is now said to be pursuing smaller deals with more partners. Netflix declined to comment.
Potential Talent Implication: Xbox reportedly asked for $800 million against Netflix's $500 million for a seven-year exclusive and is now taking smaller deals with more partners, which puts more game titles in front of more buyers.
The Facts
  • Belloni, citing three sources: Bajaria offered to license Xbox titles exclusively from Microsoft for film and TV adaptations at $500 million for seven years.
  • Xbox's Asha Sharma and her business affairs team countered at $800 million.
  • With Bajaria gone, the Netflix offer has been taken off the table. Chief financial officer Spence Neumann was among those who thought it too rich.
  • Xbox is said to be pursuing smaller deals with more partners.
  • Xbox statement: it has received record-breaking interest in its IP, calls Netflix a valued partner and cites the forthcoming Minecraft and Diablo animated series with Netflix. Netflix declined to comment.
  • Belloni expects incoming chief content officer Peter Rice to pursue more IP deals to bring in franchises.
· Puck · Matthew Belloni · 2026-10-23 · https://puck.news/what-if-peter-rice-doesnt-change-netflix-all-that-much/ · Provenance: trade-rumor source ↗
A24 Is Making UK and Australian Audiences Wait a Month for Its Record-Opening Documentary
You Can See Everything opened to $15.6 million in the US, the second-biggest documentary opening behind Fahrenheit 9/11, but A24 does not release it in the UK and Australia until November 20.
Variety reports that A24 is holding Nathan Fielder's Elizabeth Holmes documentary out of the UK and Australia until November 20, more than a month after the US opening. A24 self-distributes outside North America in only a few territories, including the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand. Sony acquired the film for Germany, Latin America and South Korea and has announced no dates. A24 declined to comment. Palace Cinemas in Australia has broken its single-day pre-sales record, at twice the level of Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour.
Potential Talent Implication: A filmmaker with backend on this film is paid on international grosses that start when A24 and Sony set the dates, and Australian pre-sales that doubled the Eras Tour record show what a month of delay holds back.
The Facts
  • US opening: $15.6 million, second-biggest documentary opening behind Fahrenheit 9/11 (Variety).
  • UK and Australia release: November 20 (A24). Sony acquired Germany, Latin America and South Korea; no release plans announced.
  • A24 self-distributes outside North America only in a couple of territories, notably UK/Ireland and Australia/New Zealand.
  • Primetime (Robert Pattinson) opened in the US on September 25 with $19.2 million, A24's third-biggest opening after Backrooms and Civil War; UK previews start October 28, days before its US VOD launch.
  • Club Kid opens in the US on November 6 and in the UK on January 8, 2027. Everything Everywhere All at Once reached the UK two months after the US in 2022.
  • Marty Supreme opened in the UK less than a week after the US and grossed more than $22 million there, A24's biggest UK result.
  • Palace Cinemas (25 locations) set a single-day pre-sales record for the film, doubling the previous holder, Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour (Variety).

Peter Rice Is Said to Favor Less Netflix Spending on Video Podcasts, Games and Creators
Netflix's incoming chief content officer is said to favor less investment in video podcasts, games and YouTube-style creators, and neither co-CEO mentioned podcasts or games on the October 20 earnings call.
Puck's Matthew Belloni reports that Peter Rice, who starts as Netflix chief content officer next week, is said to favor less investment in video podcasts, games and YouTube-style creators, categories Belloni says diluted the premium Netflix brand. He doubts they disappear entirely. Co-CEO Ted Sarandos described the core of the service on the October 20 call as differentiated, exclusive, professionally produced series, films and live events. Rice is also expected to pursue IP deals and sports rights. Netflix revenue grew 12 percent with a 34.6 percent operating margin.
Potential Talent Implication: Creators and video podcasters paid by Netflix are drawing on a budget its incoming content chief is said to want smaller, which makes the guaranteed portion and the term of each deal the numbers that matter at renewal.
The Facts
  • Belloni: Rice is said to favor less investment in video podcasts, games and YouTube-style creators, which he calls engagement-bait content that diluted the premium Netflix brand.
  • Belloni does not expect those categories to go away entirely.
  • Sarandos on the October 20 earnings call: the core of the service is delivering differentiated, exclusive, professionally produced series, films and live events. Belloni notes neither Sarandos nor Greg Peters mentioned podcasts or games on the call.
  • Netflix revenue grew 12 percent year over year with an operating margin of 34.6 percent in Tuesday's earnings (Belloni).
  • Rice is expected to pursue more IP deals and sports rights; Belloni notes the NFL, NBA and UFC are locked into long-term deals and football packages do not come up in a significant way until after the 2029-30 season.
  • Sarandos has also cited new ways to bring in third-party content, including the TF1 partnership in France.

Hunger Games Producer Nina Jacobson Says the Team Used AI Approximations of Actors to Test ADR Lines
Jacobson said the Sunrise on the Reaping team tried new line readings with AI approximations of the actors before recording them with the cast, and that none of it appears onscreen.
At IndieWire's Future of Filmmaking Summit on October 22, producer Nina Jacobson said the team on The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, which Lionsgate releases November 20, used AI approximations of actors to try new line readings for ADR (dialogue re-recorded after filming). The cast then recorded the lines in the usual way. Jacobson called AI a tool for artists that does not replace them, and said the team would never use it onscreen because the voices are not the actors.
Potential Talent Implication: A Lionsgate film used AI approximations of its actors' voices to test lines in post-production, which puts consent and payment for a voice copy used only in testing in the same conversation as the copy that reaches the screen.
The Facts
  • Jacobson: the team used AI approximations of actors to try ADR lines before recording them with the cast; the AI was used in production and post-production but never to replace artists or anything seen onscreen.
  • Jacobson: AI can duplicate a voice, and the team would still never use it onscreen because it is not their actors.
  • The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is in theaters from Lionsgate on November 20, the sixth film adaptation of the Suzanne Collins books.
  • Jacobson also discussed other Color Force projects, including a Dirty Dancing sequel with Jennifer Grey and HBO's Crazy Rich Asians series.

Documentary Producers in Rome Say Only Celebrity and Crime Films Sell Now
Dogwoof's CEO told the MIA Market that a documentary without crime or a famous subject will not work, and Dogwoof is now making microdrama-style nonfiction and a YouTube series.
Producers on an indie-documentary panel at the MIA Market in Rome said celebrity subjects and investigative stories are what sell. Dogwoof CEO Anna Godas said unless a film is crime or about someone famous, it will not work, and Dogwoof is experimenting with bite-sized nonfiction structured like microdramas and a YouTube series. THIRTEEN executive producer Stephanie Carter said the PBS station lost funding when the Trump administration pulled indirect funding to NPR and PBS in 2025, and now attaches a distributor to series or invests its own money.

The Facts
  • Lea Fels, partner and co-owner of Scenery: it is only celebrities, or a really good investigative story, that will sell.
  • Anna Godas, CEO of Dogwoof: unless it is crime or someone famous, it is not going to work. Dogwoof grew from a theatrical distributor into a full-service company.
  • Dogwoof is experimenting with bite-sized nonfiction structured like microdramas and a YouTube series called A Coffee With.

Casey Bloys Puts His HBO Executives in Charge of Both HBO Max and Paramount+ Content
Casey Bloys named his Skydance DTC content leadership, all from his HBO team, and Paramount+ originals head Jane Wiseman is leaving, with her team now reporting to Sarah Aubrey.
Deadline reports that Casey Bloys, co-chair and chief content officer of Skydance DTC, announced his leadership team two and a half weeks after the October 6 close of the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger. Francesca Orsi becomes President, HBO Drama Series and Films. Glenn Whitehead becomes President and COO of HBO and Paramount+, with oversight of business affairs, production and operations on both services. Sarah Aubrey becomes Head of Paramount+, Max Originals and International Programming. Skydance CEO David Ellison has said the two services will stay separate but bundled for a short-term phase, believed to be one to two years, before combining.
Potential Talent Implication: Paramount+ writers and producers who pitched Jane Wiseman now take projects to Sarah Aubrey, HBO drama goes through Francesca Orsi, and Glenn Whitehead runs business affairs and production for both services.
The Facts
  • Jane Wiseman is leaving as EVP and Head of Originals for Paramount+; her team reports to Aubrey.
  • Orsi was EVP, HBO Programming, Head of HBO Drama Series and Films; she will work with Bloys on which drama projects suit HBO.
  • Whitehead will also continue to guide AI initiatives for the department (Bloys memo).
  • Amy Gravitt (HBO and HBO Max comedy), Nina Rosenstein (late night and specials) and Nancy Abraham and Lisa Heller (documentaries) keep their roles; Jeff Cusson is EVP and Head of Communications, Skydance DTC.
  • Bloys said the structure is meant to keep HBO Max and Paramount+ momentum until they combine and to give the creative community clarity on where programming resides.

Two Fully AI-Acted Series Were Screened for Buyers at Mipcom
Ex Machina Studios screened finished pilots of Kira (six episodes of about 35 minutes) and Space Nation (eight of about 45) at Mipcom, with generative AI performers and human writers and directors.
LightShed Partners reports that Kira and Space Nation, two science fiction series from Ex Machina Studios, had world premiere pilot screenings last week at Mipcom 2026 in Cannes, the first fully AI-generated series shown to buyers there. All acting talent is generative AI; both series were written and directed by humans. LightShed's analysts watched the full episodes and say you quickly forget the cast is AI. They argue the cost of premium production has been the studio moat, that AI content could erode the value of studio libraries, and that platforms aggregating content, YouTube and Netflix, gain most.
Potential Talent Implication: Both series keep humans as writers and directors, so the savings from dropping actors and sets is where the terms for those two roles may now be set.
The Facts
  • Kira: six episodes of about 35 minutes. Space Nation: eight episodes of about 45 minutes. Both are finished pilots for full series, not sizzle reels.
  • Producer: Ex Machina Studios, which approved LightShed sharing the Kira trailer.
  • LightShed's view: this is the worst AI content will be; premium TV runs tens of millions of dollars per episode and films $200 million to $300 million or more.
  • LightShed named YouTube and Netflix as the likely winners among aggregators and asked whether a merged Disney+/Hulu, a combined HBO Max/Paramount+ and Peacock will become aggregators.

HBO Spent About $200 Million Setting Up Harry Potter Season One
Filings from HBO-owned Plum Jam Productions show revenue of 130.6 million pounds in 2025 against 18.4 million in 2024, putting Harry Potter season one setup near 150 million pounds, just over $200 million.
TheWrap reports that Plum Jam Productions, the HBO-owned company producing the Harry Potter series, posted revenue of 130.6 million pounds (nearly $175 million) in 2025, when production began at Warner Bros. Studios Leavesden, up from 18.4 million pounds (about $25 million) in 2024. TheWrap puts season one at just over $200 million. A person familiar told TheWrap episode budgets match House of the Dragon and The Last of Us. The filing may not show full costs, and HBO declined comment. The series debuts Christmas Day on HBO and HBO Max.
Potential Talent Implication: HBO has built infrastructure for seven seasons with two greenlit, so the option terms on actors and writers are where the gap between those numbers sits.
The Facts
  • Plan: seven seasons, one J.K. Rowling book per season; two seasons officially greenlit, with season two production starting this fall.
  • Comparison cited by TheWrap: the first Harry Potter film worked on a $125 million budget; Game of Thrones final season reportedly cost about $15 million per episode, House of the Dragon $15 million to $20 million, The Last of Us $10 million to $15 million.
  • Upfront costs include sets and infrastructure to be used across seven seasons, including a school building for child actors for the next decade.
  • Plum Jam exists to assist with U.K. filming reimbursements and has been associated with earlier productions such as The Nevers, so the filing may not show the full cost.

Hello Sunshine Sold for Under 10 Percent of Its 2021 Price, and Investors Have Moved to Creators
Candle Media valued Reese Witherspoon's Hello Sunshine at $900 million in 2021 and is selling it back for far less than 10 percent of that, while Kevin Hart has already bought out his own private equity investor.
The Ankler's Ashley Cullins tallies the early-2020s star company deals. Candle bought a majority of Hello Sunshine at a $900 million valuation and is selling it to Witherspoon and Mediawan for far less than 10 percent of that. Candle's 2022 stake valued Will Smith's Westbrook at $600 million, and Abry valued Hartbeat at about $650 million before Hart reportedly bought Abry out with Authentic Brands money. Investor Ed Simpson says the money now buys "audiences it can measure and libraries it can own," and TPG and The Chernin Group are looking at creators.
Potential Talent Implication: The 2021 prices were paid for a development slate and a famous name; the investors still writing checks want a library the company owns and an audience it can measure, and most star companies that sell their shows to studios own neither.
The Facts
  • Hello Sunshine: Candle Media (backed by Blackstone, led by Kevin Mayer and Tom Staggs) took a majority stake in August 2021 at a $900 million valuation; Witherspoon is buying it back with Mediawan for "far less than 10 percent of that number."
  • Mayer, to Semafor: Hello Sunshine is "still profitable, not terrible, but it wasn't worth what we paid."
  • Westbrook (Will Smith): Candle reportedly invested $60 million for 10 percent in January 2022 ($600 million valuation); restructured in 2024; this month announced a slate partnership with The Malar Group including 215, a scripted series about Smith's early music career. Candle still holds its stake.
  • Hartbeat (Kevin Hart): Abry Partners invested $100 million in April 2022 at about a $650 million valuation for 15 percent; in early 2026 Hart announced an Authentic Brands Group partnership and reportedly used the cash to buy back Abry's stake. Hartbeat this month signed a vertical drama first-look with Fox Entertainment.
  • Artists Equity (Ben Affleck, Matt Damon): RedBird put up "a minimum of $100 million" in November 2022; Netflix streaming feature first-look in March alongside the Sony theatrical deal; this month launched an indie film fund for emerging filmmakers.
  • Plan B (Brad Pitt): Mediawan bought a majority stake valuing it around $300 million in December 2022.
  • Mediawan (KKR-backed) owns nearly 100 labels, including Plan B, See-Saw Films, Kinetic Content and Peter Chernin's North Road Company.
  • Companies without private equity: LuckyChap, Monkeypaw, Blossom Films, Brownstone Productions; they rely on first-look or overall deals to cover overhead.
  • Ed Simpson: "In the early 2020s, Hollywood deals in general were paying for people, and now the smart money is buying audiences it can measure and libraries it can own."

Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey Is Now Universal's Highest-Grossing Film
Comcast's third-quarter theatrical revenue rose 77 percent to $1.13 billion, and Peacock posted $261 million of adjusted EBITDA, its second straight profitable quarter, with subscribers flat at 48 million.
Comcast reported third-quarter results on October 22. Universal passed $5 billion at the global box office this year, led by The Odyssey at nearly $1.9 billion worldwide and $625 million domestic. Peacock earned $261 million of adjusted EBITDA (operating profit before interest, taxes and writeoffs) on $1.8 billion of revenue. Theme park profit fell 17 percent to $780 million. Comcast says the spinoff of NBCUniversal and Sky into a standalone company run by Mike Cavanagh remains on track; Deadline notes the split is likely to draw M&A interest.
Potential Talent Implication: Nolan's film moved Universal's entire theatrical line 77 percent in a single quarter, and that is the record a filmmaker brings to the table while NBCUniversal is being separated into a company that buyers may bid for.
The Facts
  • Universal surpassed $5 billion at the global box office for the year; The Odyssey is Universal's highest-grossing film of all time, nearly $1.9 billion worldwide, $625 million domestic (Deadline).
  • Theatrical revenue: up 77 percent to $1.13 billion for the quarter.
  • Peacock: $261 million adjusted EBITDA on $1.8 billion revenue, second consecutive profitable quarter; 48 million subscribers, flat with Q2.
  • Comcast consolidated pro forma revenue about $29.3 billion, adjusted EBITDA $9.1 billion, both about flat (pro forma for the Versant spinoff).
  • Parks: profit down 17 percent to $780 million on revenue down 4.4 percent to $2.6 billion.
  • Connectivity: 144,000 domestic residential broadband net losses; 368,000 wireless line net adds; 274,000 video customer net losses.
  • NBCUniversal and Sky to be spun into a standalone company led by co-CEO Mike Cavanagh; Michael Angelakis to become Comcast CEO after the separation.
  • Comcast: "making meaningful progress on the separation of NBCUniversal and Sky, which remains on track."
  • Stock up 2.3 percent premarket; down more than 20 percent year to date.

Nathan Fielder Got A24 to Fund the Elizabeth Holmes Film With the Right to Kill It
Fielder asked A24 for money, no oversight and a provision letting him and Lance Oppenheim throw the project away at any time; the documentary has grossed an estimated $23.1 million in five days.
In 2023, after Elizabeth Holmes's own documentary deal with A24 fell apart weeks before she reported to prison, Nathan Fielder asked A24 to fund him and co-director Lance Oppenheim, leave them alone and give them a provision to kill the project at any time. A24 agreed. Oppenheim told IndieWire's Filmmaker Toolkit podcast the kill switch "changed everything." Deadline reports You Can See Everything cost under $10 million, opened to $15.6 million, won Monday and Wednesday at the domestic box office and expands to 2,600 theaters this weekend.
Potential Talent Implication: Fielder spent his leverage on control: A24 paid for a film he and Oppenheim could abandon at any point, and a $23 million first five days on a documentary made for under $10 million is the record that term now carries.
The Facts
  • Oppenheim, quoting Fielder's pitch to A24: "would you be comfortable with giving us money and essentially just leaving us alone, and giving us a provision in our deal, whatever the money was, that we could just kill it at any time?" A24 agreed.
  • Background: Holmes had approached A24 about a documentary before her May 30, 2023 prison report date; that deal fell apart (Oppenheim, via IndieWire).
  • Crew of seven; 34 days remained before Holmes reported to the federal prison camp in Bryan, Texas, when filming began.
  • Oppenheim: the kill switch "changed everything"; discussion of using it ended once they found the story.
  • Box office (Deadline): budget under $10 million; $15.6 million opening weekend, No. 2; $2.57 million Monday (No. 1); estimated $2.3 million Wednesday (No. 1); estimated five-day cume $23.1 million; expanding to at least 2,600 theaters.

Heated Rivalry Is Selling Its First Season Back to Fans in 650 Theaters
Regal, Sphere Abacus and Crave will screen all six Season 1 episodes from November 6 to 30 at $9.99 per two-episode screening in more than 650 theaters, nearly a year after the premiere.
Jacob Tierney's Crave series Heated Rivalry gets a limited theatrical run of its full first season, with distribution led by Regal at more than 275 of its locations plus AMC, Cinemark and other chains, for more than 650 theaters. Screenings pair two episodes for $9.99 and include welcome content from the cast and directors. Sphere Abacus is also taking it to the UK, Australia and New Zealand. Season 2, based on Rachel Reid's The Long Game, began production in Canada in August for a spring 2027 premiere.
Potential Talent Implication: A season fans have already streamed is now selling $9.99 tickets in 650 theaters, and whether that money reaches the creator and cast depends on how their deals defined theatrical exhibition of a series.
The Facts
  • Dates: November 6 to 30, all six Season 1 episodes, paired-episode screenings at $9.99.
  • Distribution led by Regal (275+ Regal locations); also AMC, Cinemark and other participating theaters; 650+ locations total. Partners: Sphere Abacus and Crave.

Artists Equity's Indie Label Gives the Creative Team Half the Points and Sits Outside Its Netflix and Sony Deals
Amy Baer told IndieWire that AEIP films fall below the minimum budgets in Artists Equity's Netflix and Sony output deals, so they are free to sell elsewhere, and still carry streaming viewership bonuses.
Amy Baer, president of film and television at Ben Affleck and Matt Damon's Artists Equity, said its new label, Artists Equity Independent Pictures, runs on the company's model: talent takes a smaller fee up front and equity in the film. In a typical indie, she said, half the points go to the filmmaking team and half to financiers; AEIP hands the creative team its half to divide. Because AEIP budgets sit below the minimums in the Netflix streaming and Sony Pictures theatrical output deals, those deals do not bind the label, though either buyer can still acquire a film.
Potential Talent Implication: An AEIP film pays less up front, but the creative team holds half the points and the film can sell to any buyer, which puts the value in how the points are split and what the film sells for.
The Facts
  • Label: Artists Equity Independent Pictures (AEIP), led by Jennifer Westin (formerly physical production at Topic Studios), reporting to Baer.
  • Model (Baer): "In a typical indie film, 50 percent of the points go to the filmmaking team, the other 50 percent go to the financiers. We just say to the creative team, 'Here's your points. Carve it up.' We're not going to tell you how to do it."
  • Output deals: Artists Equity has Netflix (streaming) and Sony Pictures (theatrical) output deals with minimum budget levels; AEIP films will typically fall beneath them and are not bound by either; Netflix or Sony can still buy one.
  • Bonuses: AEIP films still qualify for performance bonuses at streaming viewership thresholds, as on The Rip, where Artists Equity paid a percentage of salary to each of 1,200 crew members; thresholds and amounts undisclosed ("robust" views, "substantial" bonus).
  • First titles: A Woman in the Sun (writer-director Julia Cox; Renée Zellweger, Sissy Spacek, Mia Threapleton; Black Bear distributing) and Downriver (director Sam Jones; Garrett Hedlund, Jake Lacy, Jessica Biel).
  • Sourcing: packaged projects, not internal development; no low-budget slasher horror or experimental films.
  • Baer: "This is not a talent production company on steroids."

Agencies Want Producers to Get Their Shows Back From Streamers After Three Years
The American Entertainment Alliance would cap streamer exclusivity at three years for films and five years for series, and UTA's Rich Shuter told Puck that license fees would fall.
Puck laid out the terms of the American Entertainment Alliance plan to revive fin-syn (the old rules limiting network ownership of outside shows). Streamers with at least 10 million U.S. subscribers would spend half of original film and series budgets, excluding sports and library, with independent producers. Exclusive rights would end after three years for films; for series, two years after the third season airs, capped at five years after the first-season finale. The original streamer gets first negotiation on an extension but no right to match. The coalition has hired Akin Gump to lobby Congress.
Potential Talent Implication: The plan swaps the up-front premium for a second sale: UTA's Rich Shuter concedes streamers would pay lower license fees, and in return the producer gets the show back after three years with a library to license again.
The Facts
  • Coalition: CAA, WME, UTA, Ziffren Brittenham, Blumhouse, Imagine and Legendary among members; registered months ago at CAA's Century City address; public debut in the New York Times and on The Town.
  • Scope: streamers with at least 10 million U.S. subscribers; half of spending on original films and series, excluding sports and library acquisitions, to independent producers (companies neither owning nor affiliated with a qualifying streamer).
  • Exclusivity caps: films three years; television two years after the third season airs, outer limit five years after the first-season finale (Shuter's suggestion).
  • Extension: first negotiation right for the original streamer, no matching right.
  • Lobbying: Akin Gump retained (Lauren Rubin, Democrat; Geoff Verhoff, Republican). Pursued as separate legislation from the pending bipartisan production tax credit bill.
  • Shuter acknowledged to Puck that streamers would pay lower license fees under the plan.
  • Gardner's open questions: which agency administers it (F.C.C. or F.T.C.), who audits the 50 percent, and First Amendment exposure; cites Schurz Communications v. F.C.C. (7th Cir. 1992).

California's Tax Credit Now Backs 40 Percent of LA Location Shoots, and Production Is Still Falling
FilmLA counted 4,171 on-location shoot days in Los Angeles from July through September, down 4.8 percent from a year earlier, while credit-backed projects reached a record 40.3 percent of scripted location work.
FilmLA's quarterly report shows California's expanded credit, raised to $750 million a year from $330 million, now funds 62 percent of TV comedy and 49.4 percent of TV drama location days, up from about 20 percent each a year ago. Total shoot days are still 36 percent below the five-year average, per The Hollywood Reporter. Features rose 2.1 percent to 533 days; commercials, which the credit does not cover, fell 15.9 percent. Mayor Karen Bass called for an uncapped credit and a federal one. The program still does not count above-the-line costs.

The Facts
  • Q3 2026 (July to September): 4,171 on-location shoot days, down 4.8 percent year over year (Deadline); down about 11 percent from Q2 and 36 percent below the five-year average (THR). Q2 decline was 13 percent.

  • TV: credit-backed projects 62 percent of TV comedy and 49.4 percent of TV drama shoot days (19 percent and 20.6 percent a year ago). THR: TV 1,400 days, down about 3 percent; drama 494 days, down 9 percent; comedy 192 days, up 143 percent.

Senior Streaming Executives Leave Faster Than Studio Executives, a Count of 1,387 Appointments Finds
Stephen Follows counted 1,387 senior appointments since 2011: 17 percent of streaming appointees left within two years against 11 percent at studios, and 31 percent against 21 percent by year three.
Stephen Follows, a data analyst, pulled 11,802 trade stories from nine publications since January 2011 and tracked 531 senior appointments at streamers and 856 at studios. At the very top layer, a quarter of streaming chiefs left within two years against 14 percent at studios. HBO Max lost 30 percent of senior appointees within two years and Paramount+ 26 percent, while Netflix lost 15 percent and Amazon Prime Video 18 percent. Of 185 reported streaming exits, 22 percent used words of removal and 30 percent came with a restructure or a new boss.
Potential Talent Implication: Streaming executives leave faster than studio executives, and one in 12 reported exits mentioned a production or first-look deal, so the executive who ordered a project may be gone, or across the table as a producer, before it is delivered.

Netflix released the first official grosses in its history, $277,500 for La Bola Negra on four screens, a $69,400 per-screen average, ahead of a wider release on November 6.
Netflix's Spanish drama La Bola Negra opened to $277,500 on four screens in New York and Los Angeles, and the numbers came directly from Netflix. The film has a 45-day theatrical window and a full marketing campaign, under a new box office reporting program overseen by global theatrical distribution head Spencer Klein. Netflix called the per-screen average the second highest ever for a non-English-language film. The film expands to more markets and goes wider on November 6. Netflix has also lined up wider releases with significant windows for films from David Fincher, Greta Gerwig, Taika Waititi and others.
Potential Talent Implication: A talent deal with Netflix that pays on theatrical grosses now has a reported number to point to, which puts the length of the window and who certifies the figure at the center of the bonus language.
The Facts
  • La Bola Negra grossed $277,500 on four screens: $108,300 Friday, $84,600 Saturday, three-day per-screen average $69,400. Theaters: Paris Theater and Angelika in New York, AMC Century City and Burbank in Los Angeles.
  • Numbers came directly from Netflix on Sunday in its first official box office grosses. Netflix is giving the film a 45-day theatrical window; wider break November 6.
  • Netflix said house records: highest opening gross for a non-English-language film at the Angelika, the Paris and AMC Century City (excluding dubbed anime); second-highest per-screen average for a non-English-language film of all time; highest per-screen average ever for a Spanish film.
  • Directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi shared Best Director at Cannes. The film is Spain's Oscar entry for Best International Feature and a TIFF audience award winner. Rotten Tomatoes: 87 percent Certified Fresh.
  • Exit surveys: 96 percent Excellent or Very Good, 87 percent Definite Recommend; audience 66 percent male, 51 percent under 35.
  • Upcoming Netflix releases with wider theatrical runs and significant windows: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (David Fincher), Narnia: The Magician's Nephew (Greta Gerwig), Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory (Taika Waititi), The Mosquito Bowl (Peter Berg), Ink (Danny Boyle).
  • Variety headline the same day: "Box Office: 'La Bola Negra' Scores $277,500 From Four Theaters as Netflix Reports Grosses for First Time Ever."

  • Audience: 70 percent under 25; 56 percent male, 44 percent female; 44 percent attended with a partner.

  • Wider release next weekend, opposite DC's Clayface.

The U.K. Government Is Minded to Intervene in Sky's Takeover of ITV's Channels
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said the U.K. government is minded to intervene in Comcast's Sky purchase of ITV's networks and ITVX, which ITV agreed in July to sell for £1.6 billion.
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy told Parliament the government is "minded to intervene" in Sky's planned $2.1 billion takeover of ITV's television networks and streaming assets, citing public interest considerations. She named the need for free expression in news media, a sufficient plurality of views in news media, and a wide range of broadcasting and on-demand programs across the U.K. ITV agreed in July to sell its media and entertainment arm, including its terrestrial channels and ITVX, to Sky for £1.6 billion. ITV Studios would remain a separate company. Critics have raised concerns about the merged company's market power.
Potential Talent Implication: Two major U.K. buyers of programming would become one if the sale clears, and the government is weighing the range of programs the combined company makes available, a review that bears on how many outlets a U.K. producer can sell to.
The Facts
  • Lisa Nandy, U.K. Culture Secretary, said Thursday the government is "minded to intervene," citing news-media plurality, free expression and availability of a wide range of broadcasting and on-demand programs.
  • Deal: Sky, owned by Comcast since 2018, to acquire ITV's media and entertainment arm (terrestrial channels and ITVX) for £1.6 billion (about $2.1 billion), agreed in July.
  • ITV Studios continues as a separate company.
  • Sky CEO Dana Strong called the deal "a defining moment for British media"; ITV CEO Carolyn McCall called it a U.K. champion with scale to compete with global streamers.
  • Sky Studios, led by Cécile Frot-Coutaz, has productions including Mary & George, The Tattooist of Auschwitz and The Day of the Jackal.

Studios Want AI-Made Franchises but Cannot Copyright What AI Makes Alone
Arcos Labs founder Nelson Chu says several dozen studio executives want to make IP with AI, and his VN Studio logs which steps humans performed to support a copyright claim.
Under US copyright rules, purely AI-generated material generally cannot be copyrighted, which blocks studios from owning characters and franchises made that way. Nelson Chu, whose six-person startup Arcos Labs spoke with several dozen studio executives over months, says they want to stop others from generating their IP while generating their own with AI. Arcos's VN Studio, shown first to The Ankler, records which actions were done by AI and which by humans and screens for third-party IP. Chu does not guarantee a copyright, and the legal questions remain unsettled.
Potential Talent Implication: A studio cannot copyright what AI makes alone, so on an AI-assisted project the human work that writers, directors and artists can document could be the part that carries ownership.
The Facts
  • Source: The Ankler, Ashley Cullins, October 16, 2026, in the Dealmakers section.
  • Rule: purely AI-generated material generally cannot be copyrighted under US rules; only original works created by humans are eligible.
  • Arcos Labs: a six-person startup founded by Nelson Chu, who previously raised $50 million for the private credit startup Percent. It soft-launched this year and debuted VN in August, which it calls a fidelity recognition engine that measures how closely AI content resembles protected IP and human likenesses.
  • VN Studio: a new production platform revealed exclusively to The Ankler. It logs which actions were executed by AI and which by humans, and screens for recognizable third-party IP introduced during production. Chu will not guarantee copyright.
  • Chu: "They don't want anyone else to be able to generate their IP," describing several dozen studio executives, who added "But wait, I want to be able to generate my IP using AI."
  • A lawyer who advises studios and production companies said every studio general counsel would "fall all over themselves" for an easy tool that solves this, and that VN Studio could be "extremely pivotal" if it works as Chu describes.
  • The article notes the legal system may not give studios exclusive rights to all AI-assisted creations.

CAA, WME and UTA Are Lobbying to Require Half of Streamer Content Budgets Go to Independent Producers
The American Entertainment Alliance, with CAA, WME, UTA, Blumhouse, Imagine and Legendary as founding members, wants a law requiring big studios and streamers to put half of original content budgets into independent projects.
The American Entertainment Alliance launched October 15 with CAA, WME and UTA among its founding members, alongside producers including Jason Blum, Peter Chernin, Ron Howard and Brian Grazer. It wants Congress to require companies such as Netflix, Disney, Amazon and Skydance to spend half of their original content budgets on independent U.S. shows and movies made by non-studio entities. The proposal resembles the Financial Interest and Syndication Rules (Fin-Syn, which restricted network ownership of programming until the 1990s repeal). The New York Times first reported the group and says the companies are likely to fight any bill.
Potential Talent Implication: Under the proposal, a producer with a show outside the studio system would be selling into a pool of buyer money reserved by law, and the Times reports top producers could see bigger paydays.
The Facts
  • The group is called the American Entertainment Alliance (AEA). TheWrap says the New York Times reported it first; Deadline carries the same news the same day.
  • Deadline lists the founding members as CAA, WME, UTA, Anonymous Content, Blumhouse, Imagine Entertainment, Jeff Sagansky, Legendary Entertainment, MRC, North Road, Producers United, Propagate Content and Ziffren Brittenham.
  • TheWrap names producers Jason Blum, Peter Chernin, Ron Howard and Brian Grazer as supporters.
  • The ask is bipartisan legislation requiring major studios and streamers to devote half of their original content budgets to independent shows and movies produced in the United States by non-studio entities.
  • Companies named as targets: Netflix, Disney, Amazon and Skydance.
  • Fin-Syn limited network ownership of programming in the 1970s and 1980s and was repealed in the 1990s; series such as Hill Street Blues, The Mary Tyler Moore Show, Seinfeld and Roseanne were independently produced.
  • CAA chief Bryan Lourd: "There are fewer people deciding what gets made and what we all see, what the consumer sees... Distribution is not the issue of the future. Who finances content is the issue."
  • UTA Vice Chair Jay Sures: "As film and television increasingly consolidate, we need a regulatory framework that puts creators first, protects industry workers and preserves competition."
  • The Times says the companies have large Washington lobbying operations and will argue they already buy plenty of programming from outside studios.

The Facts

Hackman defaulted earlier in 2026 on more than $1 billion of debt tied to the lot; a Goldman Sachs-led lender takeover followed.
  • Netflix is "closing in on a deal at about a fifth of that price" (THR).
  • Four of Hackman's five major L.A. studio properties are being shopped, including Television City. An unnamed source: "In L.A., I think it's a curtain call for Hackman."
  • Property tax appeals since 2020 by the companies controlling the major lots: 269 appeals, about $319 million clawed back in decided cases; Warner Bros. Discovery, Paramount, Universal and Sony account for more than $245 million.
  • Sony Pictures Studios (Culver City): county cut about $166.3 million, an 84 percent reduction on a $198 million assessment. WBD Burbank: argued $700 million should be as low as $212 million; county cut about $51.7 million. Universal asked in 2023 to cut its assessment from $951 million to $60 million. Paramount won about $15.6 million across 14 appeals.
  • FilmLA soundstage occupancy: 90 percent (2022), 69 percent (2023), 62 percent (2025, lowest recorded). Episodic TV was about a fifth of stage production in 2023, down from about 30 percent; scripted TV shoot days fell another 23 percent in 2024.
  • Warner Bros. lot occupancy last year: 91 percent. Simon Robinson, president of global experiences and studio operations: "We were at highs effectively for all of last year."
  • New supply: East End Studios' $230 million Mission Campus (January); Cinespace six-stage Woodland Hills facility (March); Echelon, $450 million, opening later this year; FilmLA tracks seven more planned builds or renovations.

Underlying Rights Holders, Not Skydance, Decide Whether Its Franchises Can Cross Over
J.K. Rowling, Hasbro and the Tolkien estate hold the licenses behind Harry Potter, Transformers and Lord of the Rings, and IndieWire found merger-assignment language in the licensing contracts it reviewed.
IndieWire reports that the Paramount and Warner Bros. merger does not let Skydance combine its biggest franchises, because many were licensed from outside owners. Warner Bros. would need J.K. Rowling's sign-off to put her characters in another franchise; Hasbro controls Transformers; Lord of the Rings rests on a license with the Tolkien estate. Law professors Rachel Landy and Orly Ravid said the original contracts set the limits. IndieWire reviewed licenses that reassign rights to "any entity with which [the] company is merged," so creators cannot use the change of owner to take characters back.
Potential Talent Implication: Rowling, Hasbro and the Tolkien estate kept approval over where their characters can appear, so a $111 billion merger still cannot put Harry Potter beside Optimus Prime; the assignment clause in a license decides who the creator works for after the next sale.
The Facts
  • Skydance closed its $111 billion merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery this week; Ellison emphasized the combined IP at the press conference on the Warner lot.
  • Rachel Landy (Cardozo School of Law): wholly original Warner Bros. material is likely 100 percent owned and transferable; much of the marquee slate is based on books, comics, toys and dolls licensed from underlying rights holders.
  • Harry Potter: Warner Bros. can keep making films and shows but would need J.K. Rowling's sign-off to put her characters in another franchise.
  • Transformers: controlled by Hasbro. Lord of the Rings: Warner Bros. adapts under "an often contentious licensing agreement" with the Tolkien estate. Star Trek: owned outright by Paramount via the 2019 CBS merger, but not the subsequent films.
  • Orly Ravid (Southwestern Law School): "Many of the underlying rights holders negotiated for lots of protections."
  • Batman is owned outright by Warner Bros. through DC Comics; Mission: Impossible is owned by Paramount via its 1968 purchase of Desilu. Insiders at both studios dismissed live-action crossovers; one executive cited animation (The LEGO Movie model) as a possible exception.
  • No consultation needed: Warner Bros. controls Tom & Jerry, Bugs Bunny and Superman via Hanna-Barbera and DC; Paramount created Top Gun, Dora the Explorer and SpongeBob SquarePants.
  • Nearly every licensing deal includes language reassigning rights to "any entity with which [the] company is merged" (IndieWire reviewed examples).
  • 2022 precedent: Brian Robbins needed sign-off from Steven Spielberg, Hasbro and Michael Bay for the G.I. Joe coda in Transformers: Rise of the Beasts; Paramount has since dropped the Transformers and G.I. Joe crossover.
  • Landy: "Paramount has done a lot of diligence to ensure that they can exploit what they want to exploit or the deal isn't worth it."

The Federal Film Credit Has 12 Senators and Five Weeks to Pass

Training AI on a Film's Own Footage Still Runs Into the Actors' Contracts
Puck's Eriq Gardner argues InterPositive's pitch of models trained only on a production's own dailies does not clear the performers' rights embedded in that footage.
Ben Affleck sold his AI company InterPositive to Netflix for a reported $600 million; it trains models on a production's own dailies and sells the results as "clean." Puck legal columnist Eriq Gardner argues a studio can own the footage without owning the right to train on the performances in it, because actors' contracts and union agreements often do not clearly authorize machine-learning training. The same question applies to cinematographers, stunt performers, choreographers and composers. He expects guild grievances, contract disputes, and chain-of-title (proof of ownership) and insurance fights over AI-assisted work.
Potential Talent Implication: An actor's contract that is silent on machine-learning training leaves the performance in the dailies open to a studio's own-footage model, and every training license that gets signed adds evidence that those rights carry a price.
The Facts
  • Affleck, at Bloomberg's Screentime conference, said he used AI for "lots of things" on his Netflix film Animals and declined to give specifics; he sold InterPositive to Netflix for a reported $600 million.
  • InterPositive's pitch: outputs are "clean" because the model is trained on a film's own dailies.
  • Gardner: training a model "on our own stuff" is not the same as owning or having cleared every right the training implicates. Studios may own the footage and distribution rights, but performers' contracts and collective bargaining agreements often do not specifically authorize training "to create a new generation of synthetic performers."
  • Gardner: a public company making sweeping claims about airtight AI practices could invite a securities suit if the rights picture proves messier.
  • Gardner on licensing: the more companies license copyrighted material, the stronger the evidence that a market for training rights exists, which could make the fair-use defense harder over time.
  • Context: The New York Times v. Microsoft and OpenAI is at summary judgment; Anthropic paid $1.5 billion to settle with authors; Jeffrey Katzenberg has argued for a consent-and-credit model tied to Reactor, a generative video platform he invested in.
· Puck · Eriq Gardner and Ian Krietzberg · 2026-10-06 · https://puck.news/is-ethical-ai-the-future-of-hollywood/ · Provenance: analyst-inference source ↗

Germany's Production Incentive Money Ran Out in August, and Next Year's Pot Is Smaller
The DFFF and GMPF used up their €250 million for 2026 after 230 applications; waiting projects move to 2027, when the government proposes cutting the budget to €200 million.
The German Federal Film Board (FFA) told FilmFest Hamburg's Industry Days that the €250 million budget for Germany's two automatic production incentives, the German Federal Film Fund (DFFF) and the German Motion Picture Fund (GMPF), ran out in August. Applications ran 40% above the level before the rebate rose from 25% to 30% of approved German spend in 2025. Approved but unfunded projects carry into 2027, when the coalition proposes cutting the budget to €200 million, with up to €70 million reserved for features. Separately, Flanders will abolish its €3.5 million Screen Flanders fund on January 1, 2027.

The Facts
  • Combined 2026 budget for DFFF and GMPF: €250 million, exhausted in August 2026. No new applications accepted for projects planning to start principal photography in 2026.
  • Applications through the August stop: 230, which the FFA's Jolinde Sawahn says is 40% higher than before the grant rate rose from 25% to 30% at the start of 2025.
  • Projects supported in 2026 include Netflix's The Boys From Brazil, Apple TV's Wild Things, Athos 2643, Foxfinder and Gould Lover.
  • Sawahn: "We have had more applications than funds, so we're carrying over the projects we can no longer approve this year into next year," and some projects "are now facing additional costs because they have to be postponed until 2027."
  • Proposed 2027 budget: €200 million (government austerity package). Amended guidelines due next month would reserve up to €70 million for feature films; the schemes also fund high-end series.

In 2025 it invested over €4 million in 22 projects, which the fund says generated €40.2 million of local spend; Belgian producers could apply for up to €400,000 as a refundable advance. Wallimage and screen.brussels continue.

Skydance Will Run All of 2027 Without Free Cash Flow
S&P, Moody's and CreditSights put Skydance at nearly $80 billion of debt and seven times earnings, with negative cash flow projected for 2027 and Larry Ellison backstopping the 2028 and 2029 leverage targets.
Skydance, the combined Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery that formally closes October 6, starts with nearly $80 billion of debt, against about $53 billion when WBD formed in 2022. S&P Global puts leverage at seven times earnings in 2026 and 2027, with a target of three or less by 2029; if the company misses its lender targets, Larry Ellison covers the gap personally. Analysts project negative cash flow for all of 2027 and say the promised $6 billion of savings will come largely from staff cuts. Linear networks still deliver more than 70% of profit.
Potential Talent Implication: Skydance enters 2027 with no projected free cash flow and leverage targets Larry Ellison must cover personally if they are missed; upfront guarantees on projects there may be the hardest money to get until those targets are met.
The Facts
  • Debt: nearly $80 billion at close (Variety). Comparison: WBD had about $53 billion of gross debt as of June 2022 after assuming $43 billion from AT&T.
  • Close: formally set for October 6, 2026; the combined company is named Skydance.
  • Leverage: S&P Global and others calculate debt-to-earnings of 7 in 2026 and 2027; goal of 3 or less by 2029.
  • Backstop: if lender leverage targets for the end of 2028 and 2029 are missed, Larry Ellison makes up the difference from personal wealth.
  • Ratings: Moody's Ba3 (one notch below investment grade); S&P Global and CreditSights rate slightly higher, at investment grade.
  • Cash flow: projected negative for all of 2027 (Variety; S&P's Jawad Hussain: "2027 is not going to have any cash flow").
  • Savings: $6 billion of operational savings committed over three years, much of it from staff cuts.
  • Linear networks (CNN, TNT, TBS, Discovery, Nickelodeon, CBS): "70%-plus of the profits and almost all the free cash flow" (CreditSights' Hunter Martin).
  • Cost of the 12-state antitrust suit: probably another $500 million in higher interest on short-term debt (Martin).
  • Financing (Paramount Skydance IR, Sept. 30, 2026): priced $41.4 billion and EUR 885 million of senior secured notes and an $8.5 billion and EUR 850 million Term Loan B, including 6.30% senior secured first lien notes due 2028.
  • MoffettNathanson's Robert Fishman: "The company is going to be forced into choosing where to invest their dollars, led by streaming."

A Judge Threw Out Penske's Antitrust Case Over Google's AI Summaries of Its Articles
Judge Amit Mehta ruled that a publisher's expectation of search traffic is not an agreement; Penske, which owns Variety, Deadline and The Hollywood Reporter, can refile because the dismissal was without prejudice.
U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta dismissed Penske Media's suit against Google over AI Overviews, ruling Wednesday that antitrust law does not apply, TheWrap reports. Penske argued Google unlawfully conditions inclusion in search results on letting its articles feed AI summaries, said it lost revenue, and asked that Google be required to pay publishers to summarize articles or train AI on them. Mehta wrote that "an expectation is not an agreement. It is simply how a general search engine works." Mehta dismissed without prejudice, so Penske may refile.
Potential Talent Implication: A federal judge would not let Penske use antitrust law to make Google pay for AI summaries of its articles, and for creators whose work feeds AI tools, payment may now depend on a license negotiated up front.
The Facts
  • Ruling: U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta dismissed Penske Media Corporation's lawsuit against Google on Wednesday (Sept. 30); antitrust laws do not apply to AI Overviews of news articles.
  • Mehta: "Plaintiffs have pleaded only that they have an 'expectation' that Google will send them search traffic if they make their content available for free. But an expectation is not an agreement. It is simply how a general search engine works."
  • Penske's claims (filed 2025): Google leverages search by including only publishers that permit AI-summary use; about a fifth of Google searches linking to sites show Overviews; Google should be required to pay publishers to summarize articles or use them to train AI; PMC alleged lost revenue.
  • Co-plaintiff: Chegg, alleging Google illegally scraped its content.
  • Penske owns The Hollywood Reporter, Deadline, Variety, Rolling Stone, Gold Derby, Billboard, IndieWire and Artforum.
  • Dismissal was not with prejudice; Penske may refile. PMC, Google and Chegg did not immediately comment.

David Ellison named the combined Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery "Skydance" on X Friday, ahead of the $110 billion merger's expected Oct. 6 close after a year of pursuit and a two-month antitrust delay.
David Ellison announced Friday that the combined Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery will be called Skydance once their $110 billion merger closes Oct. 6, following a year-long pursuit and a two-month antitrust delay from 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America. Ellison said the name avoids favoring either century-old studio: "We never wanted a new corporate identity to diminish, alter or overshadow either one." Paramount separately priced $41.4 billion in senior secured notes and an $8.5 billion term loan B to finance the deal.   • Financing: Paramount Skydance Corporation priced $41.4 billion and €885 million in senior secured notes offerings and an $8.5 billion and €850 million term loan B facility (announced via SEC filing Sept. 30, 2026).
  • Naming history: Skydance's August 2025 acquisition of Paramount was initially styled "Paramount, a Skydance Corporation," later "Paramount Skydance Corporation." Colloquial names "WarnaMount" and "ParaBros" had circulated in the absence of an official name.
  • Discovery Communications went public in 2008; the Discovery brand will not appear in the new corporate name.

Warner Bros. Film Chiefs De Luca and Abdy Are Out
Michael De Luca and Pam Abdy learned from news reports, not a call from David Ellison, that they will not run film at the merged company, with Paramount's Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg taking over the combined unit instead.
Warner Bros. film chairs Michael De Luca and Pam Abdy will not join the merged company, Deadline and Puck reported, with Paramount's Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg set to run the combined unit's roughly 30 releases a year instead. De Luca and Abdy, under contract through 2030, could get a producing deal rather than report to the new chairs. Their Warner Bros. slate carries 56% of the combined company's 71 dated features through 2028, plus Oscar winners One Battle After Another, Sinners and Weapons, following a 2025 high and a 2026 marked by underperformers Digger, The Bride and Supergirl.

  • De Luca and Abdy have run Warner Bros.' film division since June 2022, after jumping from MGM following Amazon's acquisition of that studio; they re-upped their WBD contracts through 2030 under David Zaslav.
  • Per Deadline: neither executive received a call from Ellison about their status; they learned from news reports the night before this story published.
  • Paramount's Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg, current Paramount Motion Picture co-chairs, are poised to run the combined Paramount Warner Bros. film unit, per multiple sources.
  • The combined company inherits ~71 dated features through 2028, with 56% generated by De Luca/Abdy's Warner Bros., plus the $4.37 billion globally grossing 2025 slate they built.
  • Oscar-winning titles in that slate: One Battle After Another, Sinners (rights revert to director Ryan Coogler) and Weapons.
  • De Luca/Abdy's contracts call for them to report to the CEO, not other motion-picture chairs; reporting into Greenstein/Goldberg is described as an unlikely scenario. A producing contract at the new company is a possible alternative.
  • 2026 box office under De Luca/Abdy: no release above $100 million domestic, including underperformers The Bride and Supergirl, plus the as-yet-unreleased Digger (tracking toward a possible $30 million worldwide opening or less).
  • Under De Luca/Abdy, Warner Bros. earned 30 Oscar nominations this year (tying its 2005 record) and won 11, including Best Picture for One Battle After Another.
  • Per Puck: the executive chart for the new company is expected within days; Paramount declined to comment on De Luca/Abdy's status.

Disney had 231,000 employees at the end of fiscal 2025.

Donna Langley Says Universal Is Deliberately Undoing Its Own Short-Window Training
NBCUniversal chairman Donna Langley says Universal's move to a slate-wide 45-day theatrical window is a deliberate effort to "undo the training" it gave audiences with its pandemic-era 17-day PVOD window.
At Bloomberg's Screentime event, Langley said Universal's pivot away from the 17-day premium-VOD window it pioneered with AMC in 2020 (back to a slate-wide 45-day minimum theatrical window announced earlier this year) was driven by conversations with filmmakers and a judgment that a 17-day window undermines the moviegoing habit regardless of a film's individual box office performance. Universal and other studios, including the soon-to-be-merged Paramount-Warner, are converging on a 45-day window to premium on-demand and 90 days to streaming. Langley said the streaming window, not the PVOD window, is the one that most threatens theatrical attendance, calling unlimited in-home streaming access "an all you can eat buffet."
Potential Talent Implication: A filmmaker negotiating window length should treat the 90-day streaming threshold, not the 45-day PVOD threshold, as the term studios now consider load-bearing for theatrical health, since Langley singles it out as the one window "that could really undermine the cinemagoing habit."
The Facts
  • Universal struck a deal with AMC Theatres at the onset of COVID-19 allowing PVOD release as early as 17 days after theatrical, which triggered industry-wide windowing experimentation; Universal announced a slate-wide 45-day minimum theatrical window earlier in 2026, ending that era.
  • Langley: "I began to feel that it was time to try and reestablish that moviegoing habit in our audience, and just the simple math of it is that we can't really do that if we're telling them that it's available in the home in 17 days. It was really about signaling to the audience and trying to undo some of the training that we've done to tell them to kind of wait and watch it on their couch."
  • Universal had previously defended the 17-day PVOD window as reaching different audience types, including cost-conscious families; sources at Universal noted 2024's "The Wild Robot" still grossed $334 million after a 17-day PVOD release.
  • Universal and other studios, including the soon-to-close Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery, are converging on a general standard of 45 days to premium on-demand and 90 days to streaming.
  • Langley: "It's the streaming window that I think is the one to really keep an eye on, and we're all pretty consistent around that. That's the one that could, in my opinion, could really undermine the cinemagoing habit, because it's sort of an all you can eat buffet."

Apple Studios Visual Effects Workers Win Their First IATSE Contract
Apple Studios visual effects workers ratified their first IATSE contract, securing minimum rates, AI protections from the IATSE-AMPTP Basic Agreement, employer-paid health and retirement benefits, and overtime and rest protections matching editorial crews.
IATSE announced Apple Studios VFX workers secured their first union contract, following the same path as VFX workers on "Avatar" and at Marvel and Disney, who ratified their first contracts last year. The agreement sets minimum rates per covered title tied to annual increases matching the IATSE-AMPTP Basic Agreement, minimum-hour guarantees, pay for all hours worked, overtime including holidays and sixth/seventh workdays, employer-paid Motion Picture Industry health care and pension benefits plus a defined-contribution retirement plan (effective retroactively to all hours worked since January 1), AI protections from the Basic Agreement, turnaround and rest protections matching editorial crews, meal penalties, and hazard pay for dangerous on-set conditions. IATSE International President Matthew D. Loeb said VFX workers have long powered major productions "without the union protections afforded to many of their colleagues."
Potential Talent Implication: A second major platform's VFX workforce organizing in successive years, each contract carrying explicit AI guardrails from the Basic Agreement, establishes AI-use protections as a now-standard term below-the-line crews expect on any production regardless of which studio or platform is financing it.
The Facts
  • Apple Studios visual effects workers secured their first IATSE contract, per IATSE's September 30 announcement.
  • Contract establishes minimum rates for every covered title; annual minimum-rate increases match those negotiated in the IATSE-AMPTP Basic Agreement.
  • Workers secured minimum-hour guarantees, pay for all hours worked, and overtime protections including holidays and sixth/seventh workdays.
  • Employer-paid Motion Picture Industry health care, pension benefits, and a defined-contribution retirement savings plan; employer contributions to health/retirement plans apply retroactively to all hours worked since January 1, 2026.
  • Contract incorporates AI protections from the IATSE-AMPTP Basic Agreement, plus daily/weekly turnaround and rest protections matching editorial crews, meal penalties for violated lunch breaks, and additional pay for hazardous on-set conditions.

Endeavor's Audacious Carl Icahn Defense

Endeavor's 2025 take-private squeeze-out produced what the company calls the largest appraisal proceeding in Delaware history: roughly 80% of its public float was submitted for appraisal after shares jumped on TKO's value post-announcement. Icahn's lawyers call the new suit "procedurally bizarre."

The Facts

A Filmmaker Pitched Fox Five Meetings in One, Using AI Budget Math to Do It

Speaking at TheWrap's first AI Creator Day, FoxNXT executive vice president Jon Flynn described an unnamed creative's pitch that combined what would normally be five separate meetings into one, built entirely around AI-driven budget math: the standard budget for the feature, a roughly 15% reduction from AI tools, and a proposal to plow those savings back into production value rather than pocket them as savings. The Facts

  • Flynn described an unnamed creative who came in with a standard budget figure, told Fox they wanted to use AI tools to "rationalize about 15% of the budget," and proposed reinvesting that 15% into two additional filming locations rather than cutting the top-line number.
  • Flynn said this wasn't a one-off: filmmakers are increasingly pitching with AI-driven budget consciousness built in from the start, including using AI to add effects like explosions or to recreate speculative footage (he cited TMZ's "Celebrity Crime Scene: Princess Diana" special) more cheaply than traditional methods.
  • Flynn, a former head of AI go-to-market strategy for media at Google, said the reframing that matters most is time, not cost: a 20% aggregated time/cost savings on a six-episode series could fund a sixth episode's worth of content within the same budget.

A Federal Judge Just Set Paramount's Theatrical Release Schedule Through 2031
A federal judge approved Paramount's $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery settlement Wednesday, locking in a 30-to-32-film annual quota, 45-day theatrical windows and a $30 million penalty per film missed; the deal closes October 6.
U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín entered a consent decree Wednesday settling Paramount's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery with the states and the WGA, clearing the last obstacle to a close expected October 6. The combined company must release at least 30 theatrical films a year for two years, then 32 for three more, with minimum wide and independent release counts and at least half produced or jointly produced by the combined studio; it must hold 45-day theatrical windows and a 90-day SVOD holdback. Missing the quota costs $30 million per film, with divestiture of Paramount's Miramax stake possible if the shortfall persists. Separately, the decree requires Paramount and Warner to keep basic-cable negotiations apart (violation risks forced divestiture of BET, VH1 and Comedy Central) and creates a five-member independent board, picked by Paramount, overseeing CBS News and CNN editorial standards. The same day, Paramount confirmed former Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz will join as Co-CEO overseeing day-to-day operations and integration, starting October 6.
Potential Talent Implication: The settlement's 45-day theatrical window and per-film release quota now function as a court-enforced floor beneath any filmmaker's distribution negotiation with the combined studio, not merely a marketing promise the studio can quietly shorten.
The Facts
  • U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín entered a consent decree Wednesday, September 30, settling Paramount's $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery with the state attorneys general and the WGA; the deal is expected to close October 6.
  • Combined company must release at least 30 theatrical films a year for the first two years and 32 for the following three years; must maintain minimum numbers of wide and independent releases; at least half of films must be produced or jointly produced by the combined company.
  • Must keep 45-day theatrical windows and a 90-day SVOD holdback for qualifying films.
  • A $30 million per-film penalty applies for missing the annual quota, with divestiture of Paramount's stake in Miramax in play if the shortfall remains unaddressed.
  • Paramount and Warner Bros. must keep basic-cable negotiations separate; a violation could trigger a forced divestiture of BET, VH1 and Comedy Central, among other channels. CNN and New Line Cinema are not on the table in these divestiture scenarios.
  • The decree creates a five-member independent board, selected by Paramount, overseeing editorial standards at CBS News and CNN.
  • The court declined a temporary restraining order sought by Paramount subscribers who alleged the deal would substantially reduce competition in streaming, news and theatrical distribution.
  • Paramount announced the same day that former Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz will serve as Co-CEO of the combined Paramount-Warner Bros., starting October 6 and joining the board; Ellison remains Chairman/CEO focused on long-term strategy and creative direction while Kreiz focuses on day-to-day management and integration.
  • The approval follows Tuesday's announcement that Paramount streaming chief Cindy Holland is exiting, with HBO's Casey Bloys expected to take over the combined streaming business.

Paramount Gets the Warner Bros. Merger Without Selling a Thing
Paramount's $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery merger clears a 12-state settlement with no forced divestitures, a 45-day theatrical window, and CNN under an oversight board the Ellisons themselves will appoint.
Paramount and 12 state attorneys general settled the antitrust suit over its Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, with California's Rob Bonta dropping demands for structural remedies like a CNN sale. The deal requires a five-person CNN/CBS News editorial board appointed by the Ellisons' own board, a $1.5 billion five-year U.S. production commitment, 30 films annually (rising to 32), a 45-day theatrical window, and no requirement to keep headquarters in California.   • Deal value: $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by Paramount Skydance.
  • Settlement parties: 12 states led by California AG Rob Bonta.
  • No forced divestitures (CNN, Miramax, BET remain with the combined company); a $30 million fine per film under the 30-film annual threshold, and a Miramax divestiture, are the sole breach remedies.
  • Combined company releases at least 30 films/year for two years, then 32/year after; 20% of the slate must carry a budget of $50M+; four films per year must qualify as "independent" (originated outside the combined entity, Disney, Universal or Sony, or based on an original screenplay).
  • Theatrical window: 45 days before PVOD/SVOD; 90 days to Paramount+/SVOD.
  • Rental-term protections (no cost increase to exhibitors) hold for years 1-3 only; the protection lapses in years 4-5, when the combined studio is expected to control roughly 30% of the box office.
  • David Ellison becomes sole CEO of both studios; the studios must negotiate TV network carriage deals separately.
  • WBD shareholders receive $31/share, all cash; deal expected to close October 2026.
  • Sen. Cory Booker (D-NJ) filed a letter opposing the settlement September 24; Paramount, WBD, and the 12 settling states filed a joint response September 28 calling the objection unpersuasive.

Indie Film Buyers Have Money and Audiences. They Don't Have Enough Movies.
Top agents at CAA, UTA, WME, Gersh and 30West say a record $4.7 billion summer box office has buyers hungry for independent films, but rising costs mean there aren't enough movies to sell them.
CAA's Roeg Sutherland estimates 70% of movies in the marketplace are now independently financed even when they carry a studio logo, and buyers are competing for bespoke, festival-style films earlier than ever. Rising below-the-line costs like transport have made U.S. production prohibitively expensive, and the domestic pay-TV market that once gave indies a second life has withered. A new federal bill, introduced September 24, would create a transferable tax credit of 20-30% on labor costs, stackable with state incentives. The Paramount-WBD merger is expected to leave only one of two new specialty labels, Warners' Clockwork or Paramount's Republic Pictures, standing.
Potential Talent Implication: Agents say the fight to lower guaranteed up-front talent fees in favor of performance-based pay has quieted because both sides increasingly agree that just getting the movie made matters more, shifting real leverage in specialty film deals toward structures that pay out on results.
The Facts
  • Summer 2026 box office hit a record $4.7 billion.
  • CAA's Roeg Sutherland: "I would say that 70 percent of the movies in the marketplace are independent, in one form or another... most things right now are being financed by outside money," even when a studio logo appears on the release.
  • Curry Barker's "Obsession," bought by Focus Features out of TIFF for $15 million, went on to gross $519 million globally, the highest-grossing festival acquisition of all time.
  • Olivia Wilde's "The Invite" sold to A24 for a reported $12 million in a Sundance bidding war and grossed $60 million worldwide; Lance Oppenheim's Robert Pattinson-led "Primetime" opened to just above $19 million domestically on a $15 million budget.
  • The Motion Picture Television and Entertainment Revitalization Act, introduced September 24 in the House and Senate, would create a transferable federal tax credit on labor costs (including above-the-line talent) starting at 20%, rising to 30% for indie projects and rural/disaster-zone shoots; stackable with state incentives; $1 million minimum spend.
  • WME's Deb McIntosh argues studios/streamers benefiting from the tax credit should be required to spend a share of content budgets licensing independently produced third-party film and TV to rebuild the post-theatrical secondary licensing market.
  • Paramount-WBD merger settlement commits the combined studio to $5 million annually for an independent-film acquisition fund and four theatrical releases per year of qualifying independent films (5-year term); one dealmaker called the commitment "ridiculous," saying: "I don't blame Paramount. I blame whoever thought this was a useful win for us."
  • The merger is expected to leave one of two new studio-funded specialty labels standing: Warners' Clockwork (led by former Neon CMO Christian Parkes) has acquired Sean Baker's "Ti Amo!," Park Chan-wook's "The Brigands of Rattlecreek" (Matthew McConaughey, Pedro Pascal, Austin Butler, Tang Wei) and "Nasty" (Mary Bronstein/Rose Byrne); Noah Baumbach left Netflix for a first-look deal at Warners under the Clockwork banner.
  • Paramount's Republic Pictures, led by Lia Buman, bought StudioCanal's "The Midnight Library" (Florence Pugh) out of Cannes for $36 million.

A New Bill Would Let Rights Owners Get Foreign Piracy Sites Blocked in the U.S.
The bipartisan DEFEND IP Act lets content owners ask a judge to designate a foreign piracy site and order U.S. internet providers to block it; AT&T, Charter, Comcast, Cox and Verizon oppose it.
House and Senate sponsors from both parties introduced the DEFEND IP Act on Sept. 24. A judge would decide whether a foreign site has "no commercially significant purpose" other than copyright violation; content owners could then seek an order directing U.S. internet providers to take "reasonable measures" to block it, renewable after 360 days, including for pirated live-event streams. It is the industry's first major site-blocking push since SOPA collapsed nearly 15 years ago. The Common Sense Copyright Coalition, whose members include Comcast, opposes it, citing the Supreme Court's March ruling in Cox v. Sony.
Potential Talent Implication: The order goes to whoever owns the copyright, so creators who hold their own rights would gain a direct remedy against foreign piracy, while talent paid on a studio's backend would depend on the studio choosing to use it.
The Facts
  • Bill: Deterring Extraterritorial Foreign Exploitation of Networks Damaging Intellectual Property (DEFEND IP) Act, introduced Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026.
  • Sponsors: Reps. Zoe Lofgren (D-CA), Ben Cline (R-VA); Sens. Thom Tillis (R-NC), Chris Coons (D-DE), Marsha Blackburn (R-TN), Adam Schiff (D-CA).
  • Mechanism: a judge designates a "foreign digital piracy site" (one with "no commercially significant purpose or use other than committing a violation of copyright"); the order is subject to renewal after 360 days. Content owners may then seek an order directing service providers to "take reasonable measures to prevent users in the United States" from accessing it.
  • Covers transmission of live events from foreign locations that violate copyright.
  • Applicants must show they are "likely to suffer irreparable harm"; measures must be "technically feasible and effective" and not interfere with lawful content.
  • No mandated technical method; legal immunity for ISPs; applies to large-scale foreign sites.
  • Site-blocking is in use in almost 60 countries, per supporters.
  • Opposition: Common Sense Copyright Coalition (AT&T, Charter, Comcast, Cox, Verizon), citing new burdens on broadband providers and Cox v. Sony (March 2026: an ISP is not liable "for merely providing a service to the general public with knowledge that it will be used by some to infringe copyrights").
  • Lofgren: foreign piracy operations "exploit a loophole in our law."

  • Complaint: "even a model not directly trained on Plaintiffs' recordings is informed by, and benefits from, Suno's retained unauthorized copies."

The Federal Film Credit Bill Counts Star Salaries Toward the 20 Percent
Sens. Tim Scott and Adam Schiff and four House members introduced a 20% federal credit on U.S. production compensation Thursday, above-the-line salaries included, with 5% uplifts that can reach 30%.
A bipartisan group introduced the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act on Thursday. It pays a 20% credit on compensation tied to a production, excluding residuals, and TheWrap reports that above-the-line salaries count, as they do in the UK and Canada. Uplifts of 5% each, to a 30% ceiling, go to shoots in rural opportunity zones or federal disaster areas (Los Angeles County qualifies until 2030), independent productions, shoots across 10 or more states, and studios that raise domestic output. Credits stack on state incentives. Congress is out until after the midterms; Schiff is aiming for the lame-duck session.
Potential Talent Implication: If the bill passes, a producer earns back 20 percent of star and director salaries, and up to 30 percent on an independent shot in Los Angeles, the same above-the-line credit that sent Barbie and Deadpool & Wolverine to shoot abroad.
The Facts
  • Bill: Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, introduced Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026.
  • Co-sponsors: Sens. Tim Scott (R-SC), Adam Schiff (D-CA); Reps. Linda Sanchez (D-CA), Brian Jack (R-GA), Nathaniel Moran (R-TX), Laura Friedman (D-CA). Other backers: Reps. Judy Chu, David Kustoff, Mike Carey, Tom Suozzi.
  • Base rate: 20% of compensation directly related to a production, excluding residuals (Deadline). TheWrap: above-the-line talent salaries count toward the base.
  • Uplifts (5% each, 30% maximum, per TheWrap): at least 30% of principal photography days in a rural qualified opportunity zone or federally declared disaster area; independent production; at least 50% of principal photography and $10M in qualified compensation across 10 or more states; studio increases domestic productions relative to a historical foreign base amount.
  • L.A. County was declared a federal disaster area in 2025 after the Palisades and Altadena fires and keeps the designation until 2030 (TheWrap).
  • Eligibility: total cost above $1M; 75% of production in the U.S.; post-production and VFX covered; animation covered (TheWrap). Excluded: news, live sports, talk shows, daytime dramas, social media content, advertising, corporate video.
  • Credits transferable; stack on top of state incentives (31 states have them, per TheWrap).
  • Timing: House in recess through the midterms; Schiff said the plan is to pass it in the lame-duck session, possibly attached to a major funding bill. TheWrap: bill would take effect for productions at the start of 2027.
  • TheWrap: the $1M floor excludes microbudget films like Obsession (reported $750,000 budget, more than $500M global).
  • MPA statement: passage "could inject $250 billion into the country's economy and deliver nearly 145,000 new jobs every year."
  • Christopher Nolan (DGA president): "the most significant legislative effort in a generation to promote domestic film and television production."
  • Schiff credited Trump for the momentum and said he worked with the White House, Jon Voight and Spencer Pratt.

Sony Paid for a S.W.A.T. Spinoff Itself and Renewed It Before Starz Did
